title: Saturnalia, roles reversed
hookLine: the Roman midwinter festival turned roles upside down; Seneca stayed sober and practiced poverty (Letters 18)

cards: Rome, mid-December. The streets are loud. People have swapped their formal togas for loose, bright dinner clothes.
Shops sell little clay figures and wax candles to give as presents. Gambling, usually frowned on, is allowed in public.
In some households, ancient writers tell us, the strangest thing of all: for the feast, the enslaved people of the house are served, or sit at table with the family, and the masters wait on them.
It's the Saturnalia, the festival of the god Saturn, and Seneca has some thoughts about how to spend it.

teach.h: SATURN'S GOLDEN AGE, PLAYED FOR DAYS.
teach.b: First, the festival. The Saturnalia began on December seventeenth and grew over time to several days. Romans remembered Saturn's reign as a golden age, before rich and poor, when everyone was equal.

For a few days the festival played at that: freedom of speech, gifts, roles turned upside down. It was a game, and the next week everything went back. Rome was a slave society, and that should be said plainly.
But the game admitted something: the order of things wasn't the only possible one. Second, Seneca's letter. It's December, he writes to Lucilius, and the whole city is sweating with celebration.
Should we join in, or stay apart? Don't make a show of refusing, he says, but don't lose yourself.
Keep a sober head while others are drunk. Third, his surprising suggestion.

teach.h: PLAIN FOOD: IS THIS WHAT I FEARED?
teach.b: While everyone feasts, set aside a few days to live on the plainest, cheapest food, in rough clothing, and ask: is this what I was afraid of?
Rich people sometimes did this for fun; he means it as training, so that poverty, if it came, would hold no terror. Fourth, the reversal that lasts.

teach.h: THE PEOPLE WHO SERVE US ARE PEOPLE.
teach.b: In another letter Seneca argues that the people who serve us are human beings like us, born of the same seed, under the same sky.
A Stoic tries to keep a little of the festival all year: seeing the person who brings your coffee or delivers the box as fully a person. And a look back at the week: both ways. Equal light.
Honest review. Long light, still passing. In season.

how: Some readers of Seneca mark busy festive seasons by keeping a few plain days, and by giving thanks or gifts to the people who serve them through the year.

games.q: you're Lucilius, and the whole city is feasting for the Saturnalia. what does Seneca advise?
o: join in, but keep a sober head
games.why: Letter 18: don't make yourself conspicuous by refusing, but don't lose yourself either; and try a few plain days.

practice: Picture someone who serves you in an ordinary week, the person at the counter, the driver, the cleaner, someone at home who does more than their share, and see their face clearly.
Imagine the roles reversed, with you doing their work: how would you want to be treated? Let one small thing you could give them come to mind, a real thank-you, a kindness.

wordCard.voice: Saturnalia: the Roman midwinter festival when roles were reversed, and for Seneca a time to stay sober, practice simplicity, and remember who serves us. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: roles reversed. The one who serves is a person first. A week closed, and day six hundred seventy-two.
